reading.body:
Government AI activity is now a matter of public record: federal agencies disclose what they run, GAO audits those inventories, and 2,425 state AI bills are tracked to their source.

The pattern is layered oversight. GAO reviews federal AI inventories and management, state legislation is tracked bill by bill, and international indexes from Oxford Insights, OECD.AI, and Stanford HAI compare national readiness, strategies, and policy execution. This makes government AI adoption measurable and auditable, which shapes where and how public-sector systems can operate.

What this record does not show is the physical layer. The Oxford Insights index scores infrastructure as one dimension, but no scores or infrastructure findings appear here. The data covers governance, law, and policy, not the compute, buildings, or power behind the systems being governed.

summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The most concrete measurement of government AI use in this material comes from GAO, which found that 20 of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. Most of those use cases were in the planning phase rather than in production, and in about 200 instances agencies reported they were currently using AI. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of use cases. GAO also found the underlying reporting unreliable: five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, and two inventories included AI uses that agencies later determined were not AI at all. Without accurate inventories, GAO concluded, the government's management of its own AI use is hindered by incomplete and inaccurate data.

The uses GAO describes are operational and specific: analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers, along with identifying information security threats and facilitating review of large datasets. The White House fact sheet describes a different kind of deployment, America.gov, launched as a single digital point of entry where a person can sign in, communicate in plain language, receive answers and, where authorized and technically available, complete transactions without navigating multiple agency websites. The site's own tracking notes that America.gov runs on Google Gemini and xAI Grok, draws on about 29,000 government websites, offers no public API, and bars automated agents in its terms, with Phase 1 covering information and Phase 2 planned for 2027 with Login.gov to handle applications and renewals. Covered services under the executive order are public-facing federal services serving more than 100,000 users in a 12-month period that can be accessed or applied for online, with Internal Revenue Service tax filing and national-security-sensitive services from the Department of War and the Intelligence Community excluded.

Money and oversight are unevenly distributed. GAO reports that the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. On compliance, Commerce and the General Services Administration fully implemented selected requirements, with Commerce creating a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA establishing an AI Center of Excellence, while the Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI and the Office of Personnel Management had not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work. The Office of Science and Technology Policy did not communicate its designation of which agencies were expected to fulfill specific AI requirements. Ten of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. GAO's central caution is that there is no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, so agencies cannot consistently manage it.

The regulatory picture is being written mostly at the state level. The AI laws tracker on this site reports 6,030 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database, and a comparison of 106 measures across 28 states reviewed on September 18, 2026 found that no two states wrote the same law. Only two states passed a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors, Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149; every other measure names one setting, such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom or a state agency. No state in that set created a new agency to enforce AI law. Attorneys general enforce the larger laws, often exclusively, and several states declare a violation to be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act, while insurance commissioners, licensing boards and election agencies handle their own sectors. A private right to sue is the exception and appears mainly where one identifiable person is harmed. Where stakes are personal, the recurring rule is that AI may assist but may not be the only decider: insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone, AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician, it cannot be the sole instructor of a college course or score a teacher evaluation, and New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions.

The international and research layer is mostly about readiness and governance rather than deployment counts. OECD.AI describes itself as helping countries shape trustworthy AI with the OECD AI Principles and gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI and a blog about AI policy, and notes that organisations developing advanced AI systems can participate by submitting a report to facilitate transparency and comparability of risk mitigation measures, with the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work joined under the GPAI brand. Oxford Insights says it helps governments increase the impact of their public services by empowering teams and harnessing technology, and its Government AI Readiness Index scores nearly every country on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure and public-sector adoption. Stanford HAI's AI Index, which it describes as independent and globally sourced, reports a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it, with technical capabilities improving, investment accelerating and adoption spreading while the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate and understand the technology fall behind, in a field where data transparency is declining.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to a few practical conclusions. GAO's finding that most federal use cases sit in planning and that inventories are frequently incomplete suggests the first work is knowing what you actually run and recording it accurately. The state law tracker's advice is to build to the common core: tell people when they are dealing with AI, keep a qualified person in any decision about health, employment, benefits or education, have a crisis protocol and know the age of your user if your product holds a conversation, and keep records of what the system does, because the attorney general is the enforcer you are most likely to meet. The question in each state, as that tracker puts it, is never whether you use AI but what you use it for.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI describes itself as a policy observatory that helps countries shape trustworthy AI in line with the OECD AI Principles, and says it offers access to more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI and a blog on AI policy. It invites organisations developing advanced AI systems to take part by submitting a report, saying that sharing information would help make risk mitigation measures more transparent and comparable. The observatory states that the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI combined under the GPAI brand into one integrated partnership. Its stated purpose is to help AI actors build and use systems that respect human rights and are fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure and safe.

https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index.brief: The AI Index, described as an independent program at Stanford HAI, says it collects and visualises globally sourced data on artificial intelligence for policymakers, researchers, journalists and executives. Its current edition reports that the gap is widening between what AI systems can do and how ready institutions are to manage them, with governance, evaluation and understanding frameworks lagging behind improvements in capability, investment and adoption. The program also states that transparency around data in the field is falling, which it says makes independent measurement more important. It says earlier editions were cited in newspapers including The New York Times, Bloomberg and The Guardian, drew hundreds of academic citations, and were referenced by policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union. The Index says it is led by an interdisciplinary steering committee and notes a collaboration with a researcher who founded and leads an AI and legal technology lab at The Hague University of Applied Sciences.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: This page says it tracks 6,030 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database and linked to each bill's official page. It reports comparing the enrolled text of 106 measures passed in 28 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026, and finding that no two states wrote the same law even though the same choices recur. According to the page, only Colorado's CO SB189 and Texas's TX HB149 passed broad laws reaching consequential decisions across sectors, while every other measure names a single setting such as a chatbot, political ad, insurance prior authorization, classroom or state agency. It describes a recurring rule that AI can support a decision but cannot be its sole maker, citing insurer coverage denials, therapy, college instruction and New York benefit decisions, and states that no state in the set created a new enforcement agency, with attorneys general enforcing the larger laws and several states treating violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
